To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the diversity in vertebral failure patterns is related to variations in trabecula microarchitecture and that QCT-based FE simulations of vertebral failure are limited by the lack of incorporation in these models of these variations and by the oversimplification in these models of the boundary conditions.

vertebral fracture patterns are heterogeneous and that QCT-based FE simulations can reproduce these fracture patterns only if boundary conditions are derived from DVC and if microstructural variations among vertebrae are incorporated into the simulations.

vertebral fracture is associated with large strains in the superior third of the vertebra, and that these strains are associated with spatial variations of microstructural parameters such that they tend to be higher where connectivity density is higher.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biomechanical properties and failure mechanisms of human lumbar vertebrae.
the biomechanics of vertebral fracture.
understanding how bone microarchitecture and boundary conditions influence vertebral failure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current QCT-based FE modeling of vertebral failure is still far from being able to accurately simulate the failure of a single vertebra, let alone a whole spine.
the QCT-based FE model of vertebral failure, which is widely accepted as the standard, has significant limitations.
the QCT-based FE simulations are useful for predicting the vertebral failure patterns and the load-bearing capacities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the microarchitecture is important for vertebral failure and that QCT-based FE modeling of vertebral failure should incorporate microarchitectural variations and realistic loading conditions to be accurate.

QCT-based FE modeling of vertebral fractures can be improved by accounting for the spatial variations in trabeculae connectivity density that are observed in vertebral bodies and by using boundary conditions that correspond more closely to the measured deformations of the endplates and disks.
the QCT-based FE simulations are a powerful tool to understand the vertebral failure process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

QCT-based finite element (FE)-simulations of lumbar vertebral failure are accurate only if the microstructural variations among vertebrae are taken into account and if boundary conditions are derived from measured deformations.

, to accurately predict vertebral failure, QCT-based finite element (FE)-based simulations must incorporate the variations in trabeculae microstructure that exist among vertebrae, as well as realistic boundary conditions.

the accuracy of FE models can be improved if the trabecular microstructural variations are accounted for and if the simplified boundary conditions are replaced by more realistic boundary conditions derived from DVC measurements.
